title: Follow Resources Through a Household
definition: Goods, money, time and work available for household needs.
content:
Colonial economic demands affected resources that households used for food, work and other needs. Tribute, required labor and compulsory produce delivery were different demands. To explain an effect, identify the demand first. Then ask what resources were available and what remained afterward. A payment record alone does not reveal the whole household situation.

Consider a fictional comparison. Household A begins with twelve supply tokens and Household B with seven. Each gives three under the same model demand. Nine remain for A and four for B. This does not tell us every need or cost, but it shows why equal amounts taken do not automatically mean equal burdens. The tokens are not pesos, rice measures or actual tribute rates. In a real investigation, use dated evidence about the demand, resources and needs. Do not ask classmates to disclose family finances.

Open the three clues, then choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help. Revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs another look.
clues: Identify the demand
Tribute, labor service and produce delivery should not be confused.
Compare resources
The same demand can leave households with different resources.
Model boundary
Twelve minus three is nine; seven minus three is four, in a fictional model only.
task: Two households give three tokens but begin with different supplies. What can the model show?
Equal demands can leave different resources available
Every household faced an identical burden
Three tokens was the tribute throughout Spanish rule
The model reveals every real familys needs
reason: Equal demands can leave different resources available. Twelve minus three is nine; seven minus three is four, in a fictional model only.

title: Work and Timing Affected Daily Life
definition: When an action happens in relation to other tasks or events.
content:
A demand for work could affect household tasks differently depending on when and where it occurred. Travel could increase time away. Work during a busy farming period could leave fewer people or less time for other tasks. This is a connection to investigate, not a claim that every demand produced an identical result. Ask what work was needed, who could do it and what support was available.

Our fictional calendar has eight work slots. Three are assigned to travel and required service, leaving five for the other listed tasks. The slots are not historical service days or a universal legal rule. Compare the schedule with evidence for a particular place and period before describing actual consequences. The same instruction might meet different household conditions. A finished project does not by itself prove that every worker benefited, consented or had no other responsibilities.

clues: Time away
Work and travel could reduce time for other tasks.
Conditions
Season, distance and available support affect the burden.
Calendar limit
Eight minus three leaves five model slots, not a historical labor quota.
task: What does a fictional eight-slot calendar with three slots assigned away show?
Five slots remain for the other listed tasks in that model
Every worker served eight historical days
Travel never affected household work
Every family had identical support
reason: Five slots remain for the other listed tasks in that model. Eight minus three leaves five model slots, not a historical labor quota.

title: Choices About Producing and Selling
definition: The options a person can actually use in a situation.
content:
An economic rule could shape what growers produced or where they could sell. Earlier lessons used the tobacco monopoly as a named example. Wolters describes designated districts with compulsory cultivation and official purchase. The important question here is how a rule affected available choices, not whether a grower appeared in a trading account.

Try a fictional comparison desk. Card A allows a producer to choose among several buyers. Card B requires delivery to an authorized buyer. Card B limits the choice of buyer even if it lists a payment. Payment and freedom to choose are different questions. Neither card alone tells us the full household outcome, price fairness or every local response. Use records of the particular rule and actual transaction. This exercise does not encourage tobacco use or reward students for imposing demands on others.

clues: Policy scope
Check which crop, district and period a rule covered.
Available choices
Required delivery can restrict where a producer sells.
Separate questions
Payment does not automatically prove freely chosen participation.
task: A fictional rule requires one authorized buyer but lists a payment. Which explanation fits?
Payment and choice of buyer are separate questions
Any listed payment proves complete freedom to choose
The rule covered every crop everywhere
All households necessarily gained equally
reason: Payment and choice of buyer are separate questions. Payment does not automatically prove freely chosen participation.

title: One Total Does Not Describe Everyone
definition: Ways a change can produce different outcomes for different people.
content:
A policy or trade connection could bring income to one group while another faced costs, uncertain payment or reduced choice. Government revenue, a merchants receipts and a workers household resources answer different questions. Do not treat one large total as evidence that every community benefited equally. Ask whose experience a record actually describes.

Obispados study of early galleon trade keeps household production and cargo work visible alongside goods. Use that reminder when looking at a fictional evidence desk: a merchant ledger records receipts, a makers card describes materials and labor, and a workers note raises a payment question. Compare each record within its own setting. Missing names are not proof that no one else contributed. The exercise does not establish that every merchant gained or every worker had the same loss; particular claims still need evidence.

clues: Whose total?
Identify the person or institution described by a financial total.
Work matters
Goods and trade depended on production and other work.
Compare carefully
Receipts alone do not establish equal benefits or every households outcome.
task: A government income total is used to claim all workers became wealthy. What should be checked?
Workers own payment, costs and conditions
Only whether the total sounds large
Whether every worker had one identical experience
Nothing because revenue proves equal benefits
reason: Workers own payment, costs and conditions. Receipts alone do not establish equal benefits or every households outcome.

title: People Responded to Economic Demands
definition: An action taken when facing a situation or demand.
content:
People could respond to demands in different ways, including raising complaints or organizing opposition. The NHCP marker connects Sumuroy in Palapag, Samar, with an uprising against forced labor and abuses beginning on 1 June 1649. This named example links an economic demand with a response. It does not describe every community or every persons private reason.

For a fictional source task, compare a complaint with a later decision about the same issue. The complaint identifies a reported problem; the decision may help investigate what followed. A complaint alone does not prove success, and silence in an official account does not prove universal agreement. Explain the recorded action and say what remains unknown. We do not reenact fighting or award points for harm. Your report should make peoples actions visible without inventing speeches or claiming a single response for all communities.

clues: Named response
Sumuroys Palapag case links opposition with forced labor and abuses in 1649.
Follow-up

Source limit
Missing voices do not establish agreement by everyone.
task: A complaint records a reported problem but no decision. What should a report say?
The problem was reported; the outcome still needs evidence
The complaint automatically succeeded
Everyone necessarily agreed with the rule
No response could have occurred
reason: The problem was reported; the outcome still needs evidence. Missing voices do not establish agreement by everyone.

title: Prepare Your Community Effects Report
definition: Ways a change can produce different outcomes for different people.
content: Connect the chapters five missions. Tribute concerned required payments; polo concerned labor service; bandala concerned compulsory produce delivery. Agricultural rules could restrict production and buyers. The galleon network linked goods and peoples work across places. To explain effects, ask what happened to resources, time and choices, and whose experience the evidence describes. Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. Name a demand, identify the people and setting, give a supporting clue and state a limit. Compare household needs and resources instead of treating one total as every persons experience. Label token and calendar models as models. Check a complaint separately from its outcome, and do not invent private motives. The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. If needed, return to linked learning content before practice and a retry. This is the fifth mission, but completing it does not yet complete Chapter 9 or award its final badge. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
